title: Newton's Apple Was Real. But Did It Hit His Head?
description:
Everyone has heard of Newton's apple, but did it hit his head? This episode tells only what the records hold. On April 15, 1726, the physician William Stukeley had tea with the 83-year-old Newton under apple trees in Kensington, London. His memoir manuscript, written in 1752 (published only in 1936), says just that an apple fell: no place, no year, no hit on the head. Voltaire's 1727 book and John Conduitt's drafts also say only that an apple fell; a late note in Newton's own hand says he began thinking in 1666 of gravity reaching the Moon, with no apple. The earliest "hit on the head" we have found is in the second edition, around 1740, of an anonymous pamphlet (the 1739 first edition lacks it). It cites Pemberton, but Pemberton's 1728 book has no apple. Euler wrote the same in a 1760 letter. The tree at Woolsthorpe was shown to visitors by 1806; blown down about 200 years ago, its trunk took root again and still flowers and fruits today.

Caveats: the niece line was added only in Voltaire's new edition of 1741; "hit on the head" is the earliest we have found, no more; Stukeley's diary is read as quoted by a researcher; accounts differ on when the tree fell, so we give no year; and there is no evidence Newton himself identified this tree. Sources are in the references below.

Illustrations are AI-generated; historical figures are unnamed cartoon characters, not likenesses; modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-20

ap101.text: April 15, 1726, Kensington, London: a doctor went to visit an old friend.

ap102.text: The old friend was 83, and his name was Newton.

ap103.text: They dined alone, then had tea under the apple trees.

ap105.text: As they talked, Newton said he'd first thought of gravity in just the same situation.

ap108.text: In 1752 the doctor wrote that afternoon into a manuscript, and three things are missing.

ap109.text: In old age, Newton himself noted the year he began on gravity.

ap110.text: A dozen years after he died, a reprinted pamphlet added a passage about him.

ap111.text: An old apple tree at Newton's home blew down in a gale about 200 years ago.

ap112.text: Did that apple really hit him on the head?

ap201.text: If it hit him, the other man there that day would know: Dr. Stukeley.

ap202.text: That 1752 manuscript from the start is his memoir of Newton, now at the Royal Society.

ap203.text: The manuscript spells out Newton's "same situation":

ap204.text: Once, as he sat in a contemplative mood, an apple fell.

ap205.text: He wondered: why does an apple always fall straight down? Why not sideways, or up?

ap206.text: His answer: the Earth draws it; there must be a drawing power in matter;

ap207.text: and the apple draws the Earth, too.

ap217.text: It's the closest record we have to Newton's own words; still, it's Stukeley retelling them.

ap208.text: Where did it fall? What year? Did it touch him?

ap209.text: Those are the three things the manuscript lacks:

ap211.text: and not a word about the apple hitting his head.

ap212.text: The apple appears only here in the whole text.

ap213.text: So did Stukeley go home that day and write the apple down?

ap214.text: Seems not. Remember that dinner for just the two of them?

ap218.text: A scholar of the tree quotes his diary for that day: the dinner is there, the apple isn't.

ap215.text: Once written, the manuscript waited 184 years, until 1936, to be printed.

ap216.text: But was Stukeley the only one to write this apple down?

ap301.text: No. In March 1727 Newton died; that same year, a London book in English told of this apple.

ap302.text: Its author: the French writer Voltaire, in England when Newton died.

ap303.text: He wrote: walking in his garden, Newton saw an apple fall from a tree,

ap325.text: and so had the first idea of his system of gravity.

ap304.text: This time he's walking, not sitting.

ap306.text: Not in that book. Over a decade later, in 1741, he added a line in a new edition of another book:

ap331.text: It says: one day in the country, Newton saw fruit fall from a tree and fell deep in thought:

ap332.text: what makes all things fall toward roughly the center of the Earth?

ap326.text: This niece had kept house for Newton.

ap329.text: Who else near him left records?

ap309.text: Her husband, John Conduitt, was Newton's deputy at the Mint.

ap310.text: After Newton's death he began a biography, leaving several drafts.

ap311.text: The drafts say plague had closed Cambridge, and Newton had gone home to Lincolnshire;

ap327.text: there, he saw an apple fall from a tree.

ap314.text: Either way, none of these writers say it hit his head.

ap315.text: And Newton himself? Of all his papers, did he ever write this down?

ap316.text: Remember the year old Newton wrote down himself?

ap317.text: In a note, he listed one by one what he had worked out when young;

ap318.text: At 1666 he writes: that year, I began to wonder if gravity could reach all the way to the Moon.

ap321.text: The note has the Moon, but no apple;

ap322.text: and to this day, no apple in Newton's own hand has been found.

ap323.text: So where's the earliest "hit on the head" we can find?

ap401.text: In that reprinted pamphlet from the start, printed around 1740.

ap402.text: Its first edition, London 1739, never mentions Newton from start to finish.

ap404.text: Newton's theory of gravity came as he sat under a tree and an apple fell on his head.

ap405.text: The author adds: but he had to be a mathematician;

ap406.text: otherwise, even if a whole orchard's fruit fell on him, he'd only find it heavy and hard.

ap407.text: Who does it cite for this?

ap409.text: Pemberton edited the Principia's third edition, and talked with Newton on how the theory arose.

ap410.text: So does Pemberton's own book have the apple?

ap411.text: In 1728 Pemberton published a book on Newton's ideas; its preface says Newton sat alone in a garden, thinking about gravity.

ap412.text: A garden, gravity, but no apple; the pamphlet's source doesn't contain it.

ap414.text: Is the head version found only in this pamphlet?

ap415.text: No. In September 1760, the mathematician Euler wrote to a German princess and told of Newton too.

ap416.text: He says: this great English philosopher and mathematician once lay under an apple tree in a garden,

ap417.text: when an apple fell on his head.

ap431.text: And what has that to do with the Moon?

ap419.text: Euler goes on: but the Moon didn't fall on him;

ap420.text: so he thought what kept the Moon from falling might be its motion.

ap430.text: He adds: had Newton not lain under that tree, and the apple not hit his head, we might still not know.

ap427.text: How far did this letter travel?

ap421.text: The letters were printed in 1768; the 1795 English translation still has the apple on his head.

ap428.text: But did every reader believe it?

ap422.text: A late-1700s Paris editor added a note here:

ap423.text: Newton's own account, "by thinking on it continually," seems likelier than the apple.

ap429.text: Doubts aside, by the 19th century the apple on the head was the usual story.

ap424.text: And an apple tree at Newton's home became "the one."

ap425.text: When was it first pointed out?

ap501.text: The earliest record we have is an 1806 local history: the tree still stood, and visitors were taken to see it.

ap502.text: By then Newton had been dead nearly 80 years, over 60 years after the head pamphlet was printed.

ap503.text: Did Newton himself point this tree out?

ap504.text: No evidence. A scholar of the tree thinks it was chosen because it was the only apple tree in Newton's garden.

ap508.text: Remember the gale? The fallen trunk rerooted; today it still blooms and bears fruit at the manor.

ap512.text: So, the question we began with: did that apple hit Newton on the head?

ap514.text: Whether the apple truly inspired him stays an open case;

ap515.text: Some historians think that, telling of events 60 years past, the old Newton may have been shaping his own legend.

ap517.text: But the head case is closed: the apple is recorded; the hit was added later.

ap518.text: As a kid, did you hear it hit his head?

ap519.text: We only tell what's on record. Subscribe to open the next file with us.
